title: Disqualification of candidates following a criminal conviction
p1:
A criminal conviction can do more than affect a person's reputation.

It can decide whether they are allowed to contest an election at all.

But many people are surprised to learn that not every criminal case leads to disqualification.
p2:
A common misconception is that simply having a criminal case filed against someone removes their right to contest.

The reality is different. A person is generally disqualified only after a conviction by a court, and the law considers factors such as the offence and the punishment awarded.

This means an accusation and a proven conviction are treated very differently.
p3:
The key takeaway is that electoral laws aim to balance two concerns: protecting the integrity of public office while also protecting a person's right to participate in democracy.

A court's conviction can trigger legal consequences that go beyond the sentence itself, including restrictions on contesting elections.

Knowing this difference helps voters look beyond headlines and understand how the legal process actually works.
conclusion: Should candidates with criminal convictions be permanently barred from elections, or should there be a time limit after which they can contest again?
